Chapter 2: Building a Case Amidst Denial and Obstruction
Turning raw evidence into a case for international justice? It’s never as simple as it sounds—especially in Kosovo. Imagine trying to uncover the truth in a place where denial is the norm, and obstruction is just part of daily life. That’s exactly what investigators and prosecutors faced on the ground.
Early on, it became obvious that these weren’t just isolated acts of violence. There was a much bigger plan at play—a deliberate effort to erase evidence and rewrite history. The people responsible for the crimes had learned from the past. They knew the world was watching, so they worked hard to cover their tracks. Mass graves were moved under the cover of darkness, important documents vanished, and survivors were threatened into silence. The message couldn’t have been clearer: getting to the truth would be an uphill battle.
For the legal teams at the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia—the ICTY—every single piece of evidence was a hard-fought win. Investigators would show up at a suspected crime scene, only to find it tampered with. There’s one story that really stands out: a team spent days searching for a grave locals swore had been there, but when they arrived, they realized the bodies had already been moved. The frustration was real. Each setback stung, and served as a bitter reminder of just how far those in power would go to protect themselves.
But the obstacles weren’t just physical—they were psychological, too. Many people in Kosovo had learned not to trust outsiders, especially if those outsiders were asking tough questions. Some saw investigators as nosy meddlers, others as outright threats. Building trust took patience and care. One translator, who’d grown up in the region, described the delicate dance of earning a witness’s confidence. Say the wrong thing, or make a careless gesture, and the door could slam shut before you even had a chance to step inside.
Meanwhile, pressure was mounting back at the ICTY. The world wanted answers, and fast—but the reality was so much messier. Prosecutors had to pull together cases that could actually hold up in court, even when the evidence was incomplete or compromised. Legal standards were sky-high, and the stakes were even higher. Just one mistake could mean a war criminal might walk free.
And then there was the politics. Some governments didn’t want to cooperate, worried that their own officials might be exposed. Others only offered the bare minimum—just enough assistance to avoid criticism, but never enough to really move things forward. Investigators had to navigate a maze of red tape and hidden agendas, always trying to balance competing interests.
Yet, despite all these hurdles, there was progress. Step by step, with creativity and sheer determination, the teams began to piece together what really happened. Forensic specialists matched remains to missing people. Analysts dug through intercepted communications, searching for patterns that pointed to who gave the orders. Every breakthrough—no matter how small—felt like a win, a reminder that the truth has a way of coming to light.
Of course, the work took its toll. The emotional weight of what they were uncovering was heavy. The stories of loss, of families torn apart—it was almost too much at times. But in the middle of all that pain, people found strength—in the support of their colleagues, and in the hope that, one day, their work would bring justice to those who’d lost so much.
